text: You're given a linked list where each node has an extra random pointer, which can point to any node in the list or to null. Build a deep copy of it.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — deep copy here means three separate things. Exactly n brand new nodes, values matching one to one, and every pointer in the new list points at a new node — not a single one may point back into the original. Is that third part right? Because it's the one that makes this harder than it looks.
That's exactly right. None of the new pointers may reference original nodes.

Good. Then let me name the actual difficulty. Next is easy — it only ever points forward, so by the time I need it I'm already there. But random can point anywhere. When I'm copying node zero, its random might point at node five — and the copy of node five doesn't exist yet. It might also point backward at a node I already copied, or at itself. And that's the tell. Once a pointer can reach any node, this isn't really a list problem — it's a graph deep copy. Are there any constraints on the input size? And can the list be empty?
Up to a thousand nodes, and yes, it can be empty.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be: copy a node, then recursively copy whatever its random points at. That doesn't terminate. If A's random points at B and B's points back at A, I bounce between them forever, allocating a node every bounce. And even without a cycle, a node reachable from three randoms would get copied three times, breaking the exactly n nodes rule. This problem reminds me of memoized graph traversal. I keep a map from each original node to its copy. First time I see a node: make the copy, record it, then recurse. Every time after: hand back what's in the map. That one map buys correctness — each original is copied exactly once — and termination — a backward random hits the map and returns. It's not a speedup; the algorithm doesn't work without it.

Here's the plan. One: if the node is null, return null. Two: if it's already in the map, return its copy. Three: otherwise create the copy, register it, then recurse on next and random, and return it. One thing worth flagging is the order of that last step. The registration has to happen before the two recursive calls, not after. If I build the copy, recurse, and only then insert into the map, a node whose random points at itself will recurse into copy again, find nothing in the map, and allocate another node — forever. Putting myself in the map first announces: I'm already in progress, don't come back in. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. A thin public function creates the map and calls a recursive helper that does exactly those three steps. One thing worth flagging: the map is a local variable, not a member of the class. As a member, it would survive between calls, and its keys are addresses of original nodes. Once those nodes are freed, the allocator hands the same addresses to the next list, the count check says already copied, and I return a deleted node. Running two thousand lists through one object, nineteen ninety-seven hit a stale address. And AddressSanitizer reports nothing, because it quarantines freed memory, so addresses aren't reused. A scratch table for one call has no business outliving that call.

Let's dry-run the code with four nodes, values seven, thirteen, eleven, ten, and randoms pointing at null, zero, three, one. The part that matters is the way back up. On the way down I only build nodes and follow next. Every random gets wired on the way up — and by then the whole chain is already in the map, so all three non-null randoms are hits, including the backward one from node one to node zero. Four nodes, nothing built twice. That matches. It also means a wild random never deepens the recursion: at a thousand nodes, five different random layouts all measured exactly one thousand and one frames. Corner cases: an empty list hits the null guard. One node pointing at itself — the copy points at the copy. All randoms at one node — it's still copied once.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — each node is allocated once and each of its two pointers is wired once, with constant average map operations. Space is linear, in two separate pieces: the map holds n entries, and the recursion holds up to n plus one frames. At about ninety-six bytes a frame, a thousand nodes is roughly ninety-four kilobytes — about one percent of the default stack. Oh, one more thing — if n went to ten to the fifth, that becomes about nine point four megabytes and blows the stack. I'd switch to two iterative passes: allocate every copy into the map, then wire next and random by lookup. And for constant extra space, weave each copy right after its original, so the copy of A's random is A's random's next. It's twice the code, so I'd lead with the map version.

Very good. Three things stood out. You identified this as a graph problem from the fact that one pointer can reach anywhere, and everything after that followed from the standard graph answer. You said the map provides correctness and termination, and kept those separate. Most people describe memoization purely as a speedup. And the map-as-a-member point was the strongest part — you measured the failure rate, you knew why it fails, and you knew the sanitizer would hide it. That last piece is what separates having read about a bug class from having actually hit one.
